750.title: Rahula the novice
750.hook: the boy sets out water for his father's feet, and the Buddha teaches him with the little water left in the vessel (MN 61)
750.howItsDone: The teaching to Rahula at Ambalatthika (Majjhima Nikaya 61) is taught to novices and children in some Theravada communities as a first lesson in truthfulness and in reflecting before, during and after an action.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Anuruddha thought seven thoughts alone in a grove, and the Buddha added the eighth. Your line was few wants. Did one want go by unfed? Today, a boy among the great disciples. Day seven hundred fifty.

Rahula, the Buddha's son, is a novice now, a young monk in training, and tradition says he's about seven. He's staying at a place called Ambalatthika. Toward evening he sees his father coming, and he does what a good novice does. He sets out a seat, and water for washing the feet. The Buddha sits, washes his feet, and leaves a little water in the vessel. That little water is the whole lesson plan. He turns to his son. Rahula, do you see this little bit of water left over? Yes, sir. Today is about how he taught him.
screen: `A NOVICE SETS OUT WATER.` → `A LITTLE IS LEFT.` → `DO YOU SEE THIS?`

segments.voice: First, the little left over. So little, the Buddha says, is the monk's life of one who isn't ashamed to tell a deliberate lie. It's a stark sentence for a child. But look at what carries it: water Rahula fetched himself, a few minutes ago, with his own hands. Second, the ladle moves. The Buddha throws the water away. Do you see? Yes, sir. Just so thrown away is the monk's life of one who lies without shame. Then he turns the vessel upside down. Just so overturned. Then he turns it upright again, empty. Do you see how empty and hollow it is? Just so empty. Picture after picture, all made with the same small thing, each one a question Rahula can answer. Third, the method. Notice that the Buddha never asks Rahula to agree with an idea. He asks him to look. Do you see? And the boy says yes each time, because he does see. The teaching goes into his eyes before it goes into his memory. From here, the same discourse moves on to an elephant and to a mirror, which we met last year. But it starts with the ladle. Fourth, why a child is taught this way. Truthfulness can sound like a rule from above. Here it's a vessel in a boy's hands: something that can be full or empty, kept or thrown out. It's an image that could come back to him whenever he poured water. Gentle, not because the words are soft, but because the lesson is something he can hold.
screen: `A LITTLE WATER LEFT IN THE VESSEL.` · `THROWN OUT, TURNED OVER, EMPTY.` · `NOT AGREE, BUT LOOK.` · `A LESSON HE CAN HOLD.` · then, large: `THE LADLE OF WATER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: teach a child something gently, or get ready to. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a child you know, or the child you were. Think of one thing you'd like them to understand. Kindness, honesty, patience, anything. Now, instead of the words, look for the ladle. What ordinary object in their day could carry it? A cup, a shoe, a bowl of cereal. Turn that object over in your mind, the way the Buddha turned the vessel. If no child comes to mind, do it for yourself. The bell holds the time.
Rahula the novice. The Buddha's son, a young monk in training, taught truthfulness with the little water left in a vessel. Today's word.
Your line: the ladle of water. Today, the next time you pour water, let it remind you of one true thing you said, or one you meant to say. Day seven hundred fifty.

751.title: A handful of sand
751.hook: a commentary story: each morning Rahula took up a handful of sand and wished for as much advice as there were grains in his hand
751.howItsDone: Rahula is remembered in Theravada teaching as the model of a student eager to train, and the handful-of-sand story is told to novices and lay students as a picture of welcoming correction.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Buddha taught his young son with the little water left in a vessel. Your line was the ladle of water. When you poured water, did a true word come to mind? Today, what Rahula did with his mornings. Day seven hundred fifty-one.

There's a sentence that can make a stomach drop: can I give you some feedback? Rahula, the commentaries say, went looking for it. Every morning, the story goes, he stepped out of his dwelling, bent down, and scooped up a handful of sand. Then he made a wish over it. May I receive today, from the Blessed One and from my teachers, as much advice as there are grains of sand in my hand. Not as much praise. Not as much comfort. As much advice. A boy who asks to be corrected, every day, by the handful. Today is about that wish.
screen: `A DREADED QUESTION.` → `A HANDFUL EACH MORNING.` → `AS MUCH ADVICE AS THIS.`

segments.voice: First, the list he's on. In the Anguttara Nikaya, the Buddha names disciples who stand out, each for one quality. Rahula is named foremost among those who love the training. Not the wisest, not the strongest. The one who most wants to learn. The handful of sand is the commentary's way of showing what that looks like on an ordinary morning. Second, why it's harder than it sounds. Advice means someone has noticed what you're doing wrong. It's easy to want the teaching and skip the correction. Rahula turns it around. He treats correction as something to be gathered, like alms, like water. Third, living close to a teacher. In a short discourse in the Sutta Nipata, the Buddha asks Rahula a pointed question: does living with a wise man all the time make you look down on him? It's a real danger. Familiarity can make a teacher ordinary, and their advice easy to wave away. Rahula says no, he honors the one who holds up the torch for people. The sand is that answer, lived out every morning. Fourth, what the story is asking of an ordinary day. A handful of sand is a lot of grains. Nobody could actually receive that much advice in a day, and the story knows it. The point isn't the number. It's the open hand. Rahula wakes up already willing to be told. Last year we heard how his learning ended, with full awakening. The commentaries say this is how it went, day by day: with sand.
screen: `FOREMOST IN LOVING THE TRAINING.` · `CORRECTION, GATHERED LIKE ALMS.` · `DON'T LET CLOSENESS DULL THE TEACHER.` · `AN OPEN HAND EACH MORNING.` · then, large: `AS MUCH AS SAND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: ask for one piece of advice, or get ready to. Settle, and let the breath slow down by itself. Open one hand on your knee, palm up, as if it held sand. Now bring to mind someone whose view you trust, and who sees you clearly. A friend, a parent, a coworker, a teacher. Think of one question you could ask them: what's one thing I could do better? Notice what the body does when you imagine their answer. Then let the hand stay open anyway. The bell holds the time.
A handful of sand. Each morning, the commentaries say, Rahula wished for as much advice as the grains in his hand. Today's word.
Your line: as much as sand. Today, ask one person for one piece of advice, and when it comes, just say thank you. Day seven hundred fifty-one.

752.title: Stubborn Channa
752.hook: the old charioteer is hard to admonish; the Buddha's last instruction is that the community leave him to himself, and the silence turns him (DN 16; Vinaya, Cullavagga 11)
752.howItsDone: Theravada teachers tell Channa's story as an example of how a community's restraint, rather than punishment, can leave room for a proud person to change, and of how hard it can be to accept advice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rahula scooped up sand each morning and wished for that much advice. Your line was as much as sand. Did you ask someone for one piece? Today, a monk who wanted none at all. Day seven hundred fifty-two.

Back in year one, on the night the prince left the palace, one man was awake with him: Channa, his charioteer, who saddled the horse Kanthaka and rode out beside him. Years later Channa becomes a monk. And that's where the trouble starts. The commentaries say he couldn't forget whose friend he'd been first. It was our Buddha, our teaching, he'd say, and he brushed off the elders who tried to correct him. Then the Buddha is dying, and among the last things he tells Ananda is what should be done about Channa.
screen: `THE CHARIOTEER WHO RODE OUT WITH HIM.` → `A MONK WHO WON'T BE TOLD.` → `A LAST WORD ABOUT CHANNA.`

segments.voice: First, the instruction. In the Mahaparinibbana discourse, the Buddha tells Ananda that after he has gone, Channa should receive the higher penalty, the brahmadanda. What is it, Ananda asks. Let Channa say whatever he likes, the Buddha says, but the monks should neither speak to him, nor advise him, nor instruct him. No expulsion, no scolding. Just this: the people he kept brushing off will stop trying. Second, the news arrives. The Vinaya tells what happened after the council. Ananda travels to Kosambi, where Channa is living, and tells him. And Channa, hearing that the community will no longer speak to him, falls down in a faint. The proud man, it turns out, cared very much. Third, the turn. Troubled and ashamed, the text says, he goes off to live alone. Earnest, diligent, resolute. And before long he reaches the goal the whole path points to. The man who wouldn't accept a word of advice finds the way himself, once nobody is pushing. Fourth, the lifting. Channa goes to Ananda and asks him to lift the penalty. And Ananda answers that it was lifted already, at the very moment he was freed. The silence was never meant to last past the stubbornness. It was the space he needed to soften. The story doesn't make Channa a villain. It makes him the proof. If the charioteer who argued with everyone can wake up, the story suggests, no stubbornness is out of reach. Even Channa. That closes our days with Upali, Anuruddha, Rahula and Channa. Tomorrow, the women of the order.
screen: `THE HIGHER PENALTY: LET HIM BE.` · `THE NEWS, AND A FAINT.` · `ALONE, DILIGENT, FREE.` · `LIFTED THE MOMENT HE WOKE.` · then, large: `EVEN CHANNA.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: soften one stubborn spot. Settle, and let the breath find its own rhythm. Bring to mind one place where you dig in. An argument you always have the same way. A piece of advice you keep refusing. A habit someone has named, more than once. Don't argue with it, and don't give in yet. Just set it down in front of you, the way the community finally left Channa alone with himself. Breathe beside it. Notice whether it feels as hard as it did a minute ago. The bell holds the time.
Stubborn Channa. The old charioteer who wouldn't be told, left to himself, and freed. Today's word.

Your line: even Channa. Today, when you catch yourself digging in, take one breath before you answer, and let that be your brahmadanda: a little silence, given to yourself. Day seven hundred fifty-two.

753.title: The first nun
753.hook: Mahapajapati, who raised the Buddha, opens the way for women to go forth, then asks him for a short teaching she can take away and practice (Vinaya, Cullavagga 10; AN 8.53)
753.howItsDone: Mahapajapati Gotami is honored in Buddhist traditions as the founder of the order of nuns, and her brief teaching's eight tests are taught as a way to recognize the Dhamma in any instruction.

segments.voice: Yesterday, stubborn Channa was left to himself, and the silence turned him. Your line was even Channa. Did one breath come before an answer? Today a new part begins: the women of the order, starting with the one who went first. Day seven hundred fifty-three.

She has already done the hard part. In our first year we watched Mahapajapati, the aunt who raised the Buddha after his mother died, walk to Vesali with the Sakyan women, feet swollen, covered in dust, to ask that women be allowed to go forth. We heard Ananda speak for her, and the answer finally become yes. Today picks up after the door opens. In the Vinaya, she is the first woman to receive ordination. What does someone do after she's changed everything? Mahapajapati goes back to her teacher, and asks him for something small.
screen: `THE LONG WALK, IN YEAR ONE.` → `THE DOOR OPENS.` → `AND THEN?`

segments.voice: First, her request. In the Anguttara Nikaya, Mahapajapati asks the Buddha for a teaching in brief, so that she can go off alone and practice it, diligent and resolute. Not a title. Not a place of honor. A short teaching she can carry. Second, the answer is a test. Gotami, he says, using her clan name, whatever things you know lead to dispassion, not passion; to release, not bondage; to letting go, not piling up; to few wants, not many; to contentment, not discontent; to solitude, not company; to energy, not laziness; to being easy to support, not burdensome: know for certain that this is the teaching, this is the discipline. Eight tests, each with its opposite. Notice he doesn't hand her a list of beliefs. He hands her a way to check anything. It is a tool, not a fence. And a few of those tests may sound familiar: few wants and contentment were in Anuruddha's grove four days ago. Third, her title. The same Anguttara list of outstanding disciples names her foremost among the nuns of long standing, the senior one. She went first, and she stayed. Fourth, her own words. Her verses survive in the Therigatha, the poems of the elder nuns. In them she gives thanks to the Buddha, and says that through him she was freed from much suffering. The woman who raised him calls him the one who set her free. She went first, and then she looked back and said thank you.
screen: `A TEACHING SHE CAN CARRY.` · `EIGHT TESTS FOR ANY TEACHING.` · `FOREMOST IN LONG STANDING.` · `HER THANKS, IN HER OWN VERSES.` · then, large: `SHE WENT FIRST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor a woman who went first. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a woman who opened a door you later walked through. A grandmother who left a village. A teacher who was the only woman in the room. The first in your family to go to school, to speak up, to leave. You may know her name, or only her story. Hold her in mind. If you pray, you can remember her in your own way. If you don't, simply keep her company for a minute, the way the Therigatha keeps these women's voices. The bell holds the time.
The first nun. Mahapajapati Gotami, who raised the Buddha, opened the way for women to go forth, and asked for a teaching she could carry. Today's word.
Your line: she went first. Today, tell someone about one woman who went first for you, or thank her, if you can. Day seven hundred fifty-three.

754.title: Yasodhara's path
754.hook: the oldest rules call her only Rahula's mother; the commentaries remember her as the nun Bhadda Kaccana, foremost in great insight (AN 1)
754.howItsDone: In Theravada tradition Yasodhara is remembered through the commentaries and the Apadana as the nun Bhadda Kaccana, and some communities tell her story on its own terms, as a disciple who reached awakening.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mahapajapati, the first nun, asked for a teaching she could carry, and got eight tests. Your line was she went first. Did you think of a woman who went first for you? Today, another woman from the same palace. Day seven hundred fifty-four.

A name can disappear inside a relationship. In the Vinaya, when a small boy is sent to ask his father for his inheritance, the woman who sends him isn't called by her name. She's Rahulamata: Rahula's mother. In year one we met her as Yasodhara, the wife the prince left sleeping, and we said her story doesn't end there. In those early pages she stands between two men: the husband who left, the son who followed him. So what happens when the tradition tells her story as her own? Today, the path she walked herself.
screen: `RAHULA'S MOTHER.` → `THE WIFE LEFT SLEEPING.` → `WHOSE STORY IS IT?`

segments.voice: First, what the old rules give her. In the Vinaya she appears without her name, as Rahula's mother, sending her son out to his father. It's a small part, and it leaves most of her life out. Second, a nun's name. The commentaries say that Yasodhara, too, went forth, after Mahapajapati opened the way, and that as a nun she was known as Bhadda Kaccana. The name Yasodhara belongs to the palace. Bhadda Kaccana belongs to the path. Third, a title of her own. In the Anguttara Nikaya's list of outstanding disciples, the Buddha names the nun Bhadda Kaccana foremost among those of great higher knowledge. Read with the commentaries, that's Yasodhara, and the honor isn't for being a wife or a mother. It's for what she herself came to see. She's named in that list the same way Upali and Rahula were this past week, and Mahapajapati yesterday: for her own quality. Fourth, a farewell. A later collection of verses, the Apadana, gives her a voice at the end of her life. In it she goes to the Buddha to take her leave, and speaks of her long path in her own words, as one who has arrived. It reads like a later text, full of wonders. But its point is plain. The woman the story once named only by her son is given her own last word. Her awakening isn't a footnote to his. It's hers.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say a name of its own. Settle, and let the breath be easy. Bring to mind someone who is usually introduced through someone else. Somebody's wife, somebody's mother, somebody's assistant, somebody's younger brother. Now set the relationship aside for a moment and see them on their own. What have they come to know that's theirs? What road did they walk without anyone watching? Say their own name, silently, a few times. Then just breathe with them in mind. The bell holds the time.
Yasodhara's path. Called Rahula's mother in the old rules, remembered by the commentaries as the nun Bhadda Kaccana, foremost in great knowledge. Today's word.
Your line: her own awakening. Today, call one person by their own name, not by who they belong to, and ask them about something that's theirs. Day seven hundred fifty-four.

755.title: Khema's mirror
755.hook: a commentary story: the proud queen Khema is shown a beautiful woman growing old before her eyes, and understands (Dhammapada 347 story)
755.howItsDone: Khema's story is told with Dhammapada verse 347 in Theravada teaching, and reflection on the body's aging is a traditional practice for loosening attachment, taught with care not to turn it into self-dislike.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yasodhara's path: called only Rahula's mother in the old rules, remembered as a nun of great knowledge. Your line was her own awakening. Did you call someone by their own name? Today, a queen who stayed away. Day seven hundred fifty-five.

Some people avoid the doctor because of what the doctor might say. Queen Khema avoided the Buddha for the same reason. She was the chief queen of King Bimbisara, the Dhammapada commentary says, and very beautiful, and very proud of it. She had heard that the Buddha spoke about the faults of the body's beauty, and she didn't want to hear it. So she never went. The king, who wanted her to go, found a gentle way. He had songs made about the loveliness of the Bamboo Grove, the park where the Buddha stayed, until she wanted to see it for herself. She went to see the gardens. And at the end of the path, there he was.
screen: `A QUEEN WHO STAYED AWAY.` → `SONGS ABOUT A GARDEN.` → `AT THE END OF THE PATH.`

segments.voice: First, the vision. The commentary says that as Khema approached, the Buddha caused her to see a young woman standing beside him, fanning him, more beautiful than Khema herself. And Khema thought: I've never seen anyone like her. Next to her, I'm nothing. Second, the change. As she watches, the young woman grows older. Youth passes into middle age. Middle age into old age. Gray hair, broken teeth, wrinkled skin. Then she falls, and lies still. What took a lifetime takes moments. This is Khema's mirror. Not glass. A face she envied, showing her what every face will do, her own included. Third, the verse. The Buddha speaks, and the commentary places Dhammapada verse three hundred forty-seven here. In Max Muller's old translation it says that those who are slaves to passions run down with the stream, "as a spider runs down the web which he has made himself." Notice where the trouble is. Not in the beauty. Beauty isn't the enemy in this story. The web is the clinging, and she spun it herself. Fourth, what she did with it. The commentary says Khema understood, right there, still wearing her royal ornaments, and that with the king's blessing she went forth as a nun. The Anguttara Nikaya names Khema foremost among the nuns in wisdom. The queen who stayed away so she wouldn't hear about aging became a nun remembered for her wisdom. Beauty ages. She saw it, and was free of the web.
screen: `A WOMAN MORE BEAUTIFUL THAN HER.` · `A LIFETIME PASSES IN MOMENTS.` · `A WEB YOU SPIN YOURSELF.` · `FOREMOST IN WISDOM.` · then, large: `BEAUTY AGES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at your face kindly. If there's a mirror or a phone camera nearby, you can use it. If not, picture your face in your mind. Look at it the way you'd look at someone you love who is getting older. A line by the eyes. A gray hair, or the place where one will be. Don't judge it, and don't fix it. Just notice it's changing, as Khema saw, and let the looking stay warm. Then close your eyes, and rest with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Khema's mirror. A vision of a beautiful woman growing old, which showed a proud queen the web she'd spun herself. Today's word.
Your line: beauty ages. Today, when you pass a mirror, give your face one kind look before you walk on. Day seven hundred fifty-five.

756.title: Khema answers the king
756.hook: King Pasenadi asks the nun Khema whether the Tathagata exists after death; she answers with the sand of the Ganges and the depth of the ocean, and later the Buddha answers the same (SN 44.1)
756.howItsDone: Khema's conversation with King Pasenadi is studied in Theravada teaching on the undeclared questions, and is told as an example of a nun whose understanding matched the Buddha's own.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Queen Khema saw a beautiful woman grow old in moments, and walked out of the web she'd spun. Your line was beauty ages. Did your face get one kind look? Today, Khema the nun, and a king with a hard question. Day seven hundred fifty-six.

A king on the road, with a night to fill. In the Samyutta Nikaya, King Pasenadi of Kosala is traveling between two cities and stops for the night at a small town. He wants a conversation, so he sends a man to find an ascetic or a brahmin worth talking to. The man searches and finds none. Only one person: the nun Khema, a disciple of the Buddha, whom people describe as wise, learned, and a brilliant speaker. So the king goes to her, bows, sits to one side, and asks her a hard question. When a fully awakened one dies, what happens to him? Does he exist after death?
screen: `A KING ON THE ROAD.` → `ONLY ONE TEACHER IN TOWN.` → `WHAT HAPPENS AFTER DEATH?`

segments.voice: First, four questions, one answer. Does the Tathagata, the one thus gone, exist after death? That hasn't been declared by the Blessed One, great king, Khema says. Then he doesn't exist? Not declared. Both? Neither? Not declared, each time. The king, puzzled, asks why. Second, the sand and the sea. Khema answers with a question of her own. Great king, do you have an accountant who could count the grains of sand in the Ganges? No. Could anyone measure the water in the great ocean? No, the king says. The ocean is deep, immeasurable, hard to fathom. Just so, Khema says. The one who is awakened has let go of the body, the feelings and the rest, all the things we'd use to measure him. Freed from that reckoning, he is deep, immeasurable, hard to fathom, like the ocean. Asking whether he exists after death is like asking for a count of the sea. Third, the second conversation. Later the king meets the Buddha himself and asks him the same four questions. The Buddha gives the same answers, and the same similes, the sand and the ocean. And the king says it's wonderful, how teacher and disciple agree, in meaning and in wording. Fourth, a teacher in her own right. The king's man praised her as a brilliant speaker, yet she claimed nothing of her own: not declared by the Blessed One, she said, each time. Khema didn't need the Buddha in the room. She had understood it herself, so well that his words and hers matched. Not repeating him, but seeing the same thing. And notice the sand. A few days ago, Rahula held a handful each morning, wishing for advice. Khema holds a whole river's worth, and uses it to say: some things can't be counted.
screen: `NOT DECLARED, EACH TIME.` · `SAND IN THE GANGES, WATER IN THE SEA.` · `THE TEACHER SAYS THE SAME.` · `SHE SAW IT HERSELF.` · then, large: `THE SAME ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: trust a quiet teacher. Settle, and let the breath go deep, like the ocean in Khema's answer. Bring to mind someone who taught you something without a title. A grandparent, a neighbor, a friend who simply understood. Recall one thing they said that turned out to be true. Now let the big questions you carry stay unanswered for a minute, without counting or measuring them. Just breathe, deep and hard to fathom. The bell holds the time.
Khema answers the king. The nun who told King Pasenadi that the awakened one is like the ocean, and whose answer the Buddha later gave in the same words. Today's word.

Your line: the same answer. Today, thank one quiet teacher. And look back at this week: the ladle of water, as much as sand, even Channa, she went first, her own awakening, beauty ages, the same answer. Day seven hundred fifty-six.
